headline: Midday free-electricity tariff offers meaningful household savings for those able to shift demand, with competitive market plans beating the regulated minimum
reasoning: The Australian Energy Regulator has introduced a minimum regulated offer (Solar Share / Victorian Midday Power Saver) that provides free electricity in the middle of the day in exchange for higher tariffs at other times, designed so retailers can still recover costs. IEEFA's research found that competitive market plans already on offer tend to be more attractive than the regulated minimum, with some retailers extending the free window to four hours, reducing consumption caps, or offering better off-peak rates. The key determinant of household savings is demand flexibility: roughly 40% of homes have electric hot water systems that could be timer-controlled to run during free hours, making this the most accessible near-term saving. Households without flexibility — renters on gas appliances, EV owners unable to charge mid-day — will benefit less.
quote: Yeah, that that's a really key determinant. So if you're a household that really doesn't have the ability to flex the demand, say maybe you're a renter who has gas appliances and obviously you don't have the ability to shift to electricity, you're less likely to benefit from the offer. I'd say there's a large cohort of households that probably could benefit with some sort of small changes. So around 40% of homes have an electric hot water system. And so if you can access there's an existing timer control of that system or you're able to install a low cost timer addition, that's probably the most immediate way that a lot of households could save.
episode_title: The three-hour window which could cut household bills

headline: Solar sharer tariffs offering free midday electricity could save Australian households $600–$1,000+ per year, driven by high rooftop and utility-scale solar output suppressing wholesale midday prices
reasoning: Jay Gordon explains that high solar output during midday hours has driven wholesale electricity prices very low in that window, enabling retailers to offer free electricity between roughly 11am and 2pm. Households with electric hot water systems on timers could save $600–$1,000 per year, while EV owners can further reduce running costs by charging during the free window. The regulated 'solar share offer' (or 'Victorian Midday Power Saver' in Victoria) requires all retailers in covered regions to provide the plan, though some market offers are already more competitive than the minimum. Uptake data is limited as the regulated scheme is very new, but passive opportunities such as hot water timers are seen as the most accessible entry point. Policy and consumer education improvements are needed to help households understand and act on the opportunity.
quote: So these shoulders here are tariffs are essentially an Ng plan that offers a period of free power in the middle of the day, usually between 3:00 and 4:00 hours... some of the biggest opportunities that we saw would be things like if you've got an existing electric hot water system, simply having that operating on a timer during the free window, it could say about 600 to $1000 a year. There's also opportunities for the growing number of Australians who have an electric vehicle. So those vehicles already offer lower running costs, but you can Deacon that even further if you can charge that in the middle of the day.
episode_title: The three-hour window which could cut household bills
